messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Redirection: I think of something else, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elena had always trusted her training. Twenty-nine years on the force, the last twelve as a detective, and she had learned to read a scene the way other people read a book. So when the call came in about the illegal chemical dump in the industrial district, she did what she always did: she walked in first, without waiting for HAZMAT. The warehouse was dim, the air thick with something sweet and chemical, like artificial fruit left to rot. She remembered thinking it smelled like a hospital’s basement, that clean-sterile-underneath-a-rotten-sweetness that made her wrinkle her nose. She had taken two deep breaths before her partner yelled at her to get out. That was two years ago. Now, every time she feels short of breath—walking up stairs, carrying groceries, even just lying in bed at night—she is back in that warehouse. The memory does not come as a story with a beginning and an end. It comes in pieces: the sting in her sinuses, the yellow haze of the light, the sound of her own footsteps echoing on concrete. She tries to hold onto the whole picture, but before she can, she pushes it away. It feels like she is still standing there, her lungs burning, the smell of antiseptic and sweat filling her nose, and she has to cover her face with her hands to make it stop.

The department cleared her medically after six months. Her lung function tests came back normal. But Elena does not feel normal. She has come to believe that something inside her is permanently broken, that she will never feel ordinary emotions again—no joy, no calm, just a constant low hum of readiness. Her body stays tense, as if bracing for a blow that never lands. She scans every room she enters: the corners, the exits, the faces of strangers. When a car backfires or a door slams, she flinches so hard that her coffee splashes onto her desk. She cannot stop herself from being on high alert, and she has decided that this is just how she has to live now. She has to be on guard all the time, because no one else is going to protect her.

The betrayal feels worse than the exposure. She had trusted the department to have her back, to have protocols in place. Instead, she walked into a toxic cloud because the call had been misrouted and the HAZMAT team was twenty minutes late. The people who should have kept her safe had let her down, and now she cannot be around authority figures without her stomach knotting. She avoids her lieutenant. She takes the stairs to avoid passing the uniformed officers in the hallway. She has started working cases from her laptop at home, claiming she needs quiet for paperwork, but the truth is that the sight of a badge or a duty belt makes her want to run.

Her ex-husband called last week, asking if she wanted to meet for coffee. She said she was busy. She was not busy. She was sitting on her couch, watching the door, her hands pressed over her nose and mouth. When she cannot escape a triggering smell or a sudden sound, she forces her mind elsewhere—she thinks of grocery lists, of old movie plots, of anything except the warehouse. But the redirection never lasts. The fragmented pieces always come back.

She finally called the department’s employee assistance program after a night shift when a janitor mopped the floor with bleach, and she spent forty minutes locked in the bathroom, gasping, convinced she was dying. The intake worker asked what she hoped to get from therapy. Elena said she wanted to stop being afraid of her own body. She did not say that what she really fears is that the woman who walked into that warehouse without hesitation is gone, and she does not know how to get her back.
